title: Weta CTO: AI Tools Bring Efficiency, But Tech Must Partner With Creatives
excerpt: Kimball Thurston told Netflix's Creative Asia panel at Busan that AI is delivering real production gains — and that tech companies should collaborate more with the artists using it.
body:
• Weta FX chief technology officer Kimball Thurston told Netflix's Creative Asia panel at the Busan International Film Festival that AI tools are bringing real efficiencies to production — but have clear limitations.
  • His message to the tech industry: "Tech companies should collaborate more with creatives."
  • On the same panel, "The Outlaws" director Kang Yun-sung said AI workflows could cut feature-film budgets by 30 to 40%, while Netflix's Sung Q Lee said the streamer has used AI in some form on around 300 titles.
  • For VFX artists, animators, and filmmakers — including the large Indian creative workforce feeding global VFX pipelines — the debate is shaping what the next decade of the job looks like.

AI tools are making film production faster and cheaper, but they have hard limits — and the companies building them need to work more closely with the artists using them. That was the message from Kimball Thurston, chief technology officer at Weta FX, speaking at Netflix's Creative Asia day at the Busan International Film Festival on October 10.

Thurston joined Korean filmmaker Kang Yun-sung ("The Outlaws," "Run to the West") and Sung Q Lee, Netflix's senior director of APAC production, for the panel "AI in Filmmaking: New Tools, New Possibilities," moderated by film critic Youn Sung-eun and co-hosted by Netflix and the Motion Picture Association. The three agreed that AI is delivering genuine efficiencies in production workflows — and that its limits are just as real.

"Tech companies should collaborate more with creatives."

— Kimball Thurston, CTO, Weta FX

Context & Background

The panel was part of Creative Asia, Netflix's flagship initiative for emerging Asian creators, now in its third year and held this time at Dongseo University's Centum Campus in Busan. For the first time, the program added hands-on workshops giving aspiring writers direct access to Netflix content executives.

https://x.com/DEADLINE/status/2108861336138699121

Weta FX — the Wellington visual effects studio co-founded by Peter Jackson — sits at the center of the industry's AI reckoning. The studio has been developing custom AI tools for VFX production with partners including Amazon Web Services, deliberately designing tools meant to give artists interactive control over complex workflows rather than chatbot-style text prompts. Its stated policy is to train AI models only on its own data, rights-managed external datasets, and synthetic assets — a direct answer to the industry's loudest anxiety about scraped training data.

Impact & Analysis

Thurston's framing — efficiencies yes, limitations yes, and collaboration as the missing piece — lands differently coming from a CTO whose studio both builds and uses the tools. The panel's numbers showed how far adoption has already gone: Kang said AI workflows could take 30% to 40% off a feature film's production budget, and Lee disclosed that Netflix has used AI in one form or another on some 300 titles.

The limits Thurston flagged reflect what practitioners keep repeating: generative tools widen the options for a shot, but artists decide which options serve the story. A separate Busan session echoed the point, with Netflix's in-house VFX chief James Rustad arguing that generative AI still needs artists' judgment. For the industry's creative workforce — including the thousands of Indian animators, compositors, and VFX artists in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Mumbai studios who work on Hollywood pipelines — the question is not whether AI arrives, but whether it arrives as a tool they control or a process that replaces them.

What's Next

Creative Asia's new workshops put the collaboration Thurston called for into practice, pairing emerging Asian writers with Netflix executives. Weta's tool-building continues under its artist-in-control philosophy. The broader industry negotiation — over training data, credit, and who the efficiency gains accrue to — is only beginning.
